systemsMapSummary: Compliance is highest after patient contact (74%) and lowest before it (41%), which points away from knowledge and toward the moment itself. Three things pull compliance down at the before-contact moment: time pressure on the morning round, an environment that sometimes fails (empty bed-bay dispensers with no time to hunt for a refill), and a mixed social signal, since juniors follow whether the senior gels first. A busy round, plus an empty dispenser, plus a senior who skipped, makes 'keep moving' the safest default — and Moment 1 compliance sits at 41%.
headline: If gel were always within reach, seniors modelled it first on the round, and a simple cue marked the before-contact moment, we'd likely see Moment 1 compliance move from 41% toward the 90% target without more training.

loops: Pressure loop: busy round -> skip the moment -> skipping becomes the round's norm -> even easier to skip next round.
Modelling loop: senior skips -> juniors read skipping as acceptable -> mixed norm -> seniors get no pushback -> keep skipping.

strongestBarriers.barrier: Gel is not reliably within reach at the point of care
strongestBarriers.rationale: Highest impact and highly changeable; if gel is always at the bed bay, the before-contact moment stops competing with a walk across the ward.

strongestBarriers.barrier: Senior clinicians model the moment inconsistently
strongestBarriers.rationale: High impact; when a senior gels first, juniors follow, so the cheapest cultural lever is upstream, not more training.

strongestBarriers.barrier: The before-contact moment isn't consciously registered under load
strongestBarriers.rationale: A light, well-placed cue converts existing knowledge into action at the exact moment it is needed.

barrierNarratives.point: Put alcohol gel within arm's reach at every point of care and keep it filled
barrierNarratives.narrative: Effort at the moment of contact is the dominant barrier. If gel is always at the bed bay, cleaning hands stops competing with the round — the cheapest, fastest lever, and it removes an excuse rather than adding a rule.

barrierNarratives.point: Have the senior clinician gel first and visibly at the start of the round
barrierNarratives.narrative: Juniors take their cue from seniors. A senior who gels first at the start of every round flips the ward's social signal from mixed to clear, without a poster or a lecture.

barrierNarratives.point: Add a brief before-contact cue to the morning-round routine
barrierNarratives.narrative: Even staff who know the five moments miss them under load. A simple cue anchored to the round turns memory-dependence into a reliable trigger at the busiest time.

gapLog.content: The audit is direct observation, so the Hawthorne effect may inflate the measured 52% — true unobserved compliance is unknown.
The 6-of-56 empty-dispenser finding reflects routine stocking, not a one-off supply gap.
Confirm who owns bed-bay dispenser refills — staff describe hunting for refills, suggesting no clear point-of-care restocking routine.
Healthcare assistants were excluded from the last training and are not separately audited during personal care.

discoveryActivities: Shadow 2-3 morning rounds to time the before-contact moment and see where gel is (and isn't) within reach.
A dispenser-stocking audit across all 56 bed bays over a week to measure how often bays run empty and how fast they are refilled.
Brief interviews with junior staff on how senior modelling affects whether they stop the round to gel.
Compare Moment 1 compliance on days a senior gelled first versus days they didn't, to test the modelling link.
